## CHAPTER 13
Testing and Reporting

ALTHOUGH YOU MAY TAKE every conceivable step to harden local systems and networks, that is not enough. Your security measures will be tested regularly by attackers who are trying to get access to your systems and data. A common approach taken by businesses is to perform testing to identify weaknesses in their defense and detection capabilities so those weaknesses can be remediated before they are exploited.

Any test should apply to all parts of a layered defense, from an external firewall to the passwords selected by local users. You can monitor those ports that must be open to enable network communication. But if other ports are also open, attackers can use them to penetrate local systems without your knowledge. In this chapter, you will see what ports should be open and what you can do to keep unnecessary ports closed. The challenges have increased with the proliferation of virtual systems.

If such defenses prevent legitimate users from connecting, that would defeat the purpose of security. If an attacker does break in without your knowledge, however, that person may change files on local systems. Standard commands and integrity checkers can detect such changes. There are excellent open-source and commercial tools that you can use to detect changes, potential security flaws, intrusions, and more.

## Testing Every Component of a Layered Defense

The National Institutes of Standards and Technology (NIST) has the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) that specifies five critical functions of security program: identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover. You will probably have need of systems that can at least protect and detect. You will probably hear about defense in depth or layered defense, but the reality is that no system or network is going to be able to rely exclusively on protection, which you can think about as prevention. You need to have visibility into what is happening on your systems and in your network. If there are weaknesses, you must know what they are. This means you will need to be able to identify these weaknesses or vulnerabilities in your systems and networks.

One common approach to security in networks is to use firewalls. You can configure firewalls based on the iptables command on external routers, internal routers, and individual systems. You can also configure firewalls on many individual services using application-layer firewalls. Often you will see network-based firewalls used, but there is no reason not to also use host-based firewalls, which is firewall software like iptables running on individual hosts. On Windows Systems, Windows Defender takes care of a firewall and has been a default part of the installation on Windows for many years now. Linux systems will often include iptables, but you may be responsible for configuring the iptables rules and ensuring iptables is running to protect your Linux systems.

Users are common targets for attackers, so there is still the matter of protecting user accounts. If a user account is compromised, mandatory access control systems can provide an additional layer of protection on those systems to prevent some forms of privilege escalation, for instance.

This section provides an overview of the sections that follow so you can view the big picture of what is required to test every component of a layered defense.

### Testing a Firewall

Implicit in these tests is the issue of open network ports. As noted in the opening comments of the /etc/ services file, 65,536 ports are available. Network communication normally proceeds through one of three protocols: the Transport Control Protocol (TCP), the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), or the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP). Any communication, legitimate or otherwise, must proceed through these ports using one of the noted protocols. Commands that check for open network ports, such as nmap and nc, are discussed later in this chapter. Because firewall commands may be difficult to decipher, output like the following excerpt from the nmap command may be easier to read:

![Output displayed for an n map command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM01.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-1)

Just be sure to apply the command from both inside and outside the firewall. The results may differ depending on active services and ports addressed by firewall rules.

For testing defenses, after you have applied commands such as nmap and nc, temporarily turn off any firewall on a local system. One quick way to do so is with the iptables -F command. (You will learn how to reactivate firewalls at the end of the next section.) If you have an Ubuntu system, you are probably using the Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW), whether you realize it or not. You can disable the UFW with the command ufw disable. If you are running a Red Hat-based system, you are probably using firewalld. You can stop the firewall using systemctl stop firewalld.

### Testing Various Services

It’s possible for an administrator to make a mistake with a firewall. It’s also possible for an attacker to use a command like the [nc](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-189) command to redirect traffic through an open port in a firewall. It’s likely you will have services that need to be exposed to the outside world and certainly systems inside want to talk to systems on the outside, like users who want to browse websites. This means you can’t just restrict all access to the Internet through the firewall.

The easiest way to test the protection afforded various services is with a disabled firewall. Only then can you test the effectiveness of internal protections on various services. You can then further protect such services with TCP Wrapper along with configuration rules unique to certain services. These additional configurations may include access control lists (ACLs) managed by the application.

As you read through the tests for various services, you will note the reliance on IP address–based restrictions. Yes, attackers can spoof IP addresses, including those normally found on private IP address networks. You can use firewall rules to protect against these sorts of attacks. As private addresses are, by convention, not routable on the open Internet, you can safely block any inbound communications from those private address ranges, as you can see an example of here:

![Command to safely block any inbound communications from those private address ranges.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM02.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-2)

This command appends (-A) a rule to the chain named RH-Firewall-1-INPUT. The rule is applied to network packets coming in through the network interface (-i) on device eth0\. The rule is applied to packets with a source (-s) address in the 10.0.0.0/8 network. If an incoming packet meets these conditions, the incidence of the packet is logged with the noted prefix in the log file. This just gives you an idea of the kinds of addresses being used by attackers, however. You should go one step farther with the following rule:

![An i p tables rule.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM03.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-3)

If you would rather have an error message sent to such users, substitute REJECT for DROP.

These types of filtering rules are sometimes called Martian or bogon filters. Some addresses are simply impossible to see as source addresses when they hit your network, simply because they are not routed on the open Internet. Additionally, no matter what address range you are using on the inside of your network, you can filter out packets with a source address of your address range because anything with your addresses should not be arriving from outside your network. Blocking these sorts of addresses on the edge of your network can get rid of a lot of low level noise so your other controls can focus on issues that are more problematic.

#### Testing TCP Wrapper Services

You can apply one general test to any services otherwise protected by TCP Wrapper in the /etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny configuration files. For example, the following entry in the /etc/hosts.allow file limits access to the Secure Shell (SSH) service by username and IP address. This directive limits access to user michael on the noted IP address.

![Directive that limits access to secure shell to the user michael on the noted I P address.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM04.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-4)

You should be able to test this rule by trying to log in as user kilroy from a different IP address as well as by trying to log in as a different user from the specified IP address.

#### Testing Apache

Several services feature their own configuration checkers. For example, the Apache web server includes a syntax checker in its basic control command. Depending on the distribution, the control command may be httpd or apache2ctl. The switches for these commands are the same. For example, the following command checks the syntax of Apache configuration files on an Ubuntu system:

![Command that checks the syntax of Apache configuration files on an Ubuntu system.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM05.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-5)

In contrast, if you configure virtual hosts on an Apache web server on a Red Hat system, the following command checks the syntax on each individually configured virtual host:

![Command that checks the syntax on each individually configured virtual host.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM06.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-6)

Syntax checks are a basic part of the configuration of any service. In addition, a syntax check can help you identify services that may have been modified without your knowledge.

Of course, security checks on Apache go beyond syntax. If you have configured a website that uses certificates for encryption, you should check the status of those certificates—especially if they were purchased from a certificate authority. For that purpose, you can look for an Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) server.

Normally, if you have configured password security on an Apache-based website, it will be based on usernames and passwords configured with the htpasswd command. Unless such databases have been handed off to a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) server, an Apache authentication database is typically kept in or near the same directory as Apache configuration files.

Of course, you will want to test such password-protected directories. Can users without entries in the Apache authentication database access such directories? If you navigate directly to the protected directory in question, the Apache server should automatically prompt for a username and password.

One strong recommendation is to disable the use of .htaccess files. As hidden files, they do not appear in the output of a casual search. Therefore, if an attacker were to include an .htaccess file in an Apache configured directory, he or she could include directives that override any configuration you have set up. You can avoid such problems with the following directive in any Directory container:

![Command that disables the use of the dot h t access files.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM07.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-7)

#### Testing Samba

As with Apache, one issue with respect to Samba is the syntax. If there is a problem, Samba may not be available to your users, violating that tenet of the C-I-A triad of confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The testparm command provides an excellent syntax check for a Samba configuration file. The output, shown in [Figure 13-1](#9781284255935_CH13_01.xhtml_c13-fig001), is straightforward.

![Testing Samba syntax.](images/9781284255935_CH13_FIGF01.jpg)

FIGURE 13-1 Testing Samba syntax with testparm.

[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-fig13-1)

If there is a problem with basic Samba security options, this output should reveal it. For example, the following option in the [homes] stanza reveals the existence of user home directories to any user who connects to that service:

![The option in the homes stanza that reveals the existence of use home directories to any user who connects to that service.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM08.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-8)

With a list of usernames, an attacker can get to work, especially if those users work primarily on Microsoft Windows machines.

Some Samba directories may be further limited with configuration options such as hosts allow, which limits access to the local Samba server to systems on the localhost and the noted private IP address networks:

![The configuration option, hosts allow, which limits access to the local Samba server to systems on the local host and the noted private I P address networks.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM09.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-9)

Of course, Samba security extends to connected user-authentication databases. If it’s a Windows NT–style database stored locally, you can configure the Samba server as a Primary Domain Controller (PDC). Security options are associated with that database.

That database may be stored locally in a file in the /etc/samba/ directory. Related options such as user and machine profiles are in essence Linux directories that hold Microsoft configuration files.

#### Testing Other Services

Apache and Samba are just two of the many Linux-based services available. The steps taken to test the security of those services should provide a model for testing the security of other network services that you have configured on a Linux system.

#### After Service Tests Are Complete

When you are finished testing various services, you should be able to restore the firewall with an appropriate script. On Red Hat systems, you will likely need to install the iptables-services package to get the service scripts needed. You can also use firewalld-cmd to manage the firewall. In that case, you would use firewalld rather than iptables as the service, shown here.

![Command that restarts the i p tables service.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM10.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-10)

Of course, that applies only to Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) networking. For IPv6 networking, the corresponding service is ip6tables. Although the same scripts are not available on Ubuntu systems, tools such as the Uncomplicated Firewall front end provide a script that can activate and deactivate iptables and ip6tables firewall rules. You would use the ufw command on Ubuntu systems to manage the firewall. You can use ufw reload to reload the stored rules or ufw disable and ufw enable to stop and start the firewall.

### Testing Passwords

As for passwords, a variety of open-source testing tools are available. Of the top 10 password crackers at http://sectools.org/crackers.xhtml, tools like [John the Ripper](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-134), [Hydra](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-118), and [RainbowCrack](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-233) can help you identify weak passwords, should they exist. Hydra is good for brute-forcing network services, while John the Ripper and RainbowCrack can be used for offline cracking if you have password files.

In general, you should be able to take the files with local authentication databases and test them with the noted tools. Given enough time, processing power, and direct access to such files, all such passwords can be cracked. However, the process can take days, months, or even years, depending on the tool, the hardware, and the strength of the password. If an attacker did break into a local system and could get access to local authentication databases, how long would it take for that person to crack such passwords? That and related questions are explored later in this chapter.

### Testing Mandatory Access Control Systems

If an attacker can break into a user or a service account, the next line of defense is a mandatory access control system, such as Security Enhanced Linux (SELinux) and Application Armor (AppArmor). If network services are properly protected, even a compromise in a service account would not lead to a compromise in a service.

For example, what happens if there is a compromise of the service account associated with the Apache web server? Would an attacker, masquerading as a legitimate user, be able to write to key files? Generally, if SELinux were set to enforcing mode with an httpd_sys_content_rw_t context, the answer would be yes. But is that context necessary for the files in question? Could the service still function appropriately with a context of httpd_sys_content_t? These are the tests and questions associated with mandatory access control systems such as SELinux and AppArmor.

## Checking for Open Network Ports

This section focuses on basic open-source commands related to network ports—specifically the nmap, lsof, telnet, and netstat commands. Many of the tools discussed in this chapter take advantage of these commands.

Related to these commands is netcat, the nc command, which is discussed later in this chapter. More extensive tools such as Nessus and OpenVAS, a fork of Nessus, are also covered later in this chapter.

### The telnet Command

One reason the telnet command still exists on the systems of many security administrators is its utility. It’s an easy way to check for open ports over a network. It’s worth noting this command is the telnet client and not the telnet server, which is used to accept remote connections that allow remote command line access to systems in cleartext. The telnet client can be used to initiate TCP connections to arbitrary ports that you may want to connect to. For example, suppose a colleague has set up a website, but nobody can connect to it. She says it’s up and running on her system. It’s easy to test a connection to such a website with the following command, substituting the actual hostname or IP address for host.domain.com:

![Command to test the connection to a website.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM11.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-11)

If ports between your systems are open and unblocked, you should see the following output:

![The response to the command that tests the connection to a website in case the ports between the systems are open and unblocked.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM12.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-12)

At that point, you should be able to press Ctrl+] to get the ^] character and press Enter to get to a telnet> prompt. From there, type the quit command to return to the command-line interface.

Similar commands should work with the port number for most standard services online. For example, if you run the telnet your_mail_server.domain.com 25 command (substituting the name of the target email server for your_mail_server.domain.com) and get a “Connection refused” message, a bad port number or perhaps a firewall rule may be blocking the connection to that outgoing email server. If there is no response at all, then the telnet command is likely getting through to the target server but not getting a response. That suggests nothing is listening on port 25.

One of the limitations of the telnet command is that it can connect only to systems that use TCP ports. Later, you will look at the nc command, which can connect to systems that use TCP and UDP ports.

If some server is listening on port 25, you will see it in the output of a netstat command with appropriate switches. It can also work with systems that communicate on both TCP and UDP ports.

### The netstat Command

The [netstat](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-192) command is a powerful tool. With a variety of different switches, it can help you get into and better understand the networking subsystem. It has mostly been supplanted by the ss command, though you can still install netstat and related tools. On an Ubuntu system, for example, you would install the net-tools package.

Knowledgeable Linux users may already know that the netstat -r command displays the routing table that applies to the current system. With the -n switch, the netstat command works in numeric format. In other words, it does not perform name lookups using the Domain Name Service (DNS) or the /etc/services file.

The netstat command can tell you more. The -t switch specifies TCP ports. The -u switch specifies UDP ports. With the help of the -a switch, netstat can tell you about all connections on the local system. So put those switches together. [Figure 13-2](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig002) displays the start of the output of the netstat -atun command.

This is a lot of output, indicative of a system that has a lot of network connections. This could be a result of having a lot of listening services with users connected, or it could be user activity. In general, a lot of netstat output is nothing to worry about immediately, though it could warrant further investigation. [Table 13-1](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-tbl001) describes the output, with columns listed from left to right. To see the actual column headers, you will have to pipe the output to the less command pager and then the views of the output would be limited. Alternatively, if a bastion host is configured on the local system, a view of all such listen connections can be seen in a normal output, and you will see an example of such later in this section.

With [Table 13-1](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-tbl001) in mind, take another look at the output from the netstat -atun command shown in [Figure 13-2](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig002). Review the first couple of lines of output, one at a time:

![A screenshot showing the output of the net stat hyphen a t u n command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_FIGF02.jpg)

FIGURE 13-2 Identify what your system listens to with netstat -atun.

[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-fig13-2)

TABLE 13-1 Output from netstat -atun.

| COLUMN | DESCRIPTION |
| --- | --- |
| Proto | The protocol, typically TCP or UDP. On some systems, protocols associated with IPv6 communication may be shown as TCP6 and UDP6. |
| Recv-Q | Received communication in the queue, in bytes, usually 0. |
| Send-Q | Transmitted communication in the queue that is not yet acknowledged, in bytes, usually 0. |
| Local Address | Local IP address and port number. |
| Foreign Address | Remote IP address and port number. Unless there is an established connection, this is normally set to IPv4 address and port number 0.0.0.0:*, which is listening for connections from any IPv4 address. It may also be set to IPv6 address and port number :::*. |
| State | Connection state, normally LISTEN or ESTABLISHED. A network service that is in the LISTEN state has not yet made a connection. |

![A t c p command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM13.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-13)

The first line is a TCP connection associated with port 139, listening for requests from systems with any IP address (0.0.0.0). This port is used for the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. This is listening because there is a Samba service running on this system. Perhaps another listening is more troublesome because the number seems really high, which would be uncommon for a typical service. Port 42829 falls into what is commonly the ephemeral range, which means they are ports that are used as needed and released, such as those used when initiating a connection from a client to a server where the initial source port isn't important, only the destination port.

![The first line in the output for the net stat hyphen a t u n command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM14.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-14)

You may be able to gather more information by using the telnet command described earlier and connecting to port 42829:

![A telnet command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM15.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-15)

Because the localhost address is normally associated with 127.0.0.1 in the /etc/hosts file, that connection should work. Try it again with the IP address of the local adapter.

If the netstat status is true, the connection to the IP address of the local adapter should be refused. The same command, when run from a remote system, may lead to a message that suggests that the connection was refused, typical of a block by an iptables-based firewall.

If you are wondering what service is listening on any of the ports listed, you can add another switch to the netstat command. By adding a p, you are telling netstat you want the name and process ID of the listening program. Those same two lines look like this when we add the p switch.

![Output when the p switch is added to the net stat hyphen a t u n command.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM16.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-16)

The lines in the screen shown in [Figure 13-2](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig002) go on for some time. That number of network connections suggests a very active system, and a number of services are certainly listening. Keep in mind, the more services you have listening, the more target area attackers have to compromise your system using a technical attack. In contrast, take a look at [Figure 13-3](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig003), where the netstat -atun command is applied system with far fewer network connections, suggesting this server doesn’t offer much in the way of services, so it has a much smaller attack surface.

![A screenshot showing the output of the net stat hyphen a t u n command on a bastion server.](images/9781284255935_CH13_FIGF03.jpg)

FIGURE 13-3 The netstat -atun command on a bastion server.

The displayed output is easier to explain. The first line, which specifies port 22, is associated with an SSH server. The second line, associated with the localhost address and port 25, illustrates a Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) server such as Postfix or sendmail that is not yet listening to anything from a regular network address. Take a closer look at the second line, associated with an ESTABLISHED connection:

![The second line in the output that is associated with an ESTABLISHED connection.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM17.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-17)

It’s a TCP connection on port 22, from the address 192.168.178.54. This is a system on the same network as the server netstat was run from, which can be seen from the first three octets being the same. This is not a guarantee, since the networks could be very small, but in this case, the two systems are on the same network. The server communicates back to the client on port 56112.

You can also see ports associated with TCP networking over an IPv6 connection, as indicated by the tcp6 label. The one tcp6 service is the SSH service that corresponds to the IPv4 service on the top line.

The fifth line specifies an established communication over UDP port 68, normally associated with the [Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP)](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-32). (BOOTP is a protocol of the TCP/IP suite associated with the automatic assignment of IP addresses. It may also be used for the automatic acquisition of IP addresses from a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol [DHCP] server on a remote network. It’s associated with UDP port 68.) If this system can get IP address information from the local system or does not need to use DHCP, you may want to disable or even uninstall associated software. Note that the word connection was not used in the example because this is UDP. UDP does not have connections, even if netstat does maintain a list of whether there are established communications.

Now take the command a step further with the -p switch to identify the process in question. For the UDP BOOTP port just described, the process is the dhclient process, which confirms the association between that port and the DHCP client.

### The lsof Command

The [lsof](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-166) command lists open files. It can also be focused on network-related processes with the -i switch. Add the -n switch to keep IP addresses in numeric format, and you can quickly get a view of network-related processes on the local system:

![The l s o f command that lists open files.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM18.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-18)

If you have a lot of active network services, the output could be substantial. [Figure 13-4](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig004) shows one example. Compare this with the output to the netstat -atun command described earlier. Not only does the lsof -ni command organize connections by service, it also includes user and process identifier (PID) information.

![A screenshot of the output that is generated by the l s o f, hyphen n I command on a multipurpose system.](images/9781284255935_CH13_FIGF04.jpg)

FIGURE 13-4 The lsof -ni command on a multipurpose system.

### The nmap Command

The nmap command is an incredible tool. Several books have been written about this network exploration tool and port scanner. To get a taste of what it can do, run nmap by itself. Then run it on the system of your choice using an IP address or hostname. If a firewall has been configured on a system, it’s interesting to note the differences from inside and outside the firewall.

The following sections address some of the options described in the nmap output. Those commands that require root administrative privileges are preceded by the use of the command sudo, which provides temporary root privileges. It is a very bad idea to ever run as root, even if you login as your normal user and switch to the root user. Always use sudo to gain temporary elevated permissions.

nmap can take several minutes to run over a network. If you are just learning nmap, it may be faster to run the commands described in the following subsections against an IP address on your local network. Of course, if you are testing a system behind a firewall, you cannot measure the effectiveness of that firewall unless you run nmap on a system on the other side of that firewall.

In general, if you want more information in the output, the verbose (-v) switch can help. If you need still more information, the -vv switch adds even more verbosity. The description in this chapter is far from complete; several books are written solely on the intricacies of nmap.

#### Target Specification

You can target nmap at a group of systems, an IP address, a hostname, or a fully qualified domain name. For example, the following command reviews the systems with IP addresses 192.168.0.1 through 192.168.0.3:

![A listing of the n map command that reviews the systems with I P addresses 192 dot 168 dot 0 dot 1 through 192 dot 168 dot 0 dot 3.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM19.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-19)

The following command reviews all systems on the noted network, in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation:

![A listing of the n map command that reviews all systems on the noted network, in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (C I D R) notation.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM20.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-20)

#### Host Discovery

An attacker with access to a private network might start with a ping scan. In the following command, the -s switch scans and the -P switch applies the ping command to the systems on the target addresses:

![A listing of the n map command with the hyphen s switch for scanning and the hyphen P switch for applying the ping command to the systems on the target addresses.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM21.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-21)

It just takes a few seconds to display a list of active systems on that network. One other useful switch from this section is the -n switch, which avoids the use of DNS servers for name resolution. If there is an excessive delay when running other nmap commands, the -n switch may help.

Although such a command saves time, not all hosts respond to requests made with the ping command. The following command scans all hosts in the noted network:

![A listing of the n map command that scans all hosts in the noted network.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM22.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-22)

The command is time-consuming. It could easily take several hours to scan all the ports on all the IP addresses on the noted network. That is just for the 254 allowable IP addresses on that network. That process would take a lot longer for the 16,000,000 IP addresses on the class A private network, 10.0.0.0/8.

#### Scan Techniques

Although nmap focuses on TCP packets, network communication also uses UDP packets. To scan a system for open UDP ports on a given IP address, run the following command:

![A listing of the n map command that scans a system for open U D P ports on a given I P address.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM23.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-23)

Of course, network communication can proceed through more than just the TCP and UDP protocols. To find the full list of protocols enabled for an IP address, run the following command:

![A listing of the n map command that finds the full list of protocols enabled for an I P address.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM24.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-24)

#### Port Specification and Scan Order

One of the idiosyncrasies of nmap is that it scans only most commonly used ports. The number of ports checked varies depending on the version of nmap used. For example, version 5.00 checks 1,000 ports by default. For some, however, that is an incomplete scan. The -p switch can help; the following scan checks all 65,536 TCP/IP ports:

![A listing of the n map command that checks all 65,536 T C P I P ports.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM25.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-25)

Of course, because that scan just applies to TCP ports, you may also be interested in the following command, which builds on the switches described in a previous section to check UDP ports:

![A listing of the n map command that builds on the previous command that checks U D P ports.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM26.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-26)

#### Service Version Detection

With the -sV switch, nmap searches for the version number of all services communicating over open ports. [Figure 13-5](#9781284255935_CH13_02.xhtml_c13-fig005) shows the output of the nmap -sV -p 0-65535 192.168.178.10 command. Note how it lists all open services and their version numbers. An attacker who looks at this output and is aware of weaknesses of older versions of certain servers may pounce on this information.

![Output of an n map command that displays a list of open services with version information.](images/9781284255935_CH13_FIGF05.jpg)

FIGURE 13-5 A list of open services with version information.

[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-fig13-5)

Of course, as a security professional, you can use this information to help identify information that has been exposed to the outside world. If your scan includes version information in the results, which it shouldn’t, you may be able to determine whether there are outdated services that need updating. This information may also reveal ports that you may close, perhaps by uninstalling or disabling a service. Alternatively, you could close these ports with appropriate firewall commands if they are only needed locally.

#### Operating System Detection

The operating system detection option, -O, may reveal the operating system associated with the target machine. This is not always going to give you great results. As an example, running it against an Ubuntu server system running up-to-date software yielded a guess by nmap that it was a FortiGate firewall. You will get a percentage chance that it is correct if it is guessing. In this case, there is a 92 percent chance it is a FortiGate. It is not, of course. A scan of another Linux system returned the following results, showing it is a running a current version of the Linux kernel.

![A scan of a Linux system with results indicating that it is running a current version of the Linux kernel.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM27.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-27)

#### Scripts

There is a scripting engine that comes with nmap, based on the Lua programming language. In addition to a scripting engine, the nmap installation includes dozens of scripts you can use to gather additional information. The scripts fall into several categories. These categories will be described shortly. Some scripts may fall under multiple categories. Because new scripts and even new switches are under development, assume this is a partial list. There may be a dozen or more scripts available in several of these areas.

Running scripts with nmap is easy. You just use the -script parameter and include the script you want to run. You can also run multiple scripts at the same time, either by listing them or by using wildcards. For example, a command like the following applies all scripts associated with a scan of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) service:

![A listing of the n map command that applies all scripts associated with a scan of the H T T P service.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM28.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-28)

If the given script is misspelled or is not otherwise available, nmap should return an error with the following message related to the script:

![The error message that is displayed by n map if the given script is misspelled or is not otherwise available.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM29.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-29)

Some of the scripts described appear only in beta versions of nmap. Although the use of beta software is normally discouraged in production software, it can give you more tools to detect security issues as they are created by attackers.

##### Authentication (auth).

nmap authentication scripts test usernames, passwords, and more on target systems, possibly through a brute-force attack. You can use authentication scripts for networked services associated with a number of protocols. These protocols range from the Apple Filing Protocol (AFP) to Telnet. For example, the following command attempts a brute-force attack to guess usernames and passwords on the FTP server on the noted IP address:

![n map command that attempts a brute-force attack to guess usernames and passwords on the F T P server on the noted I P address.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM30.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-30)

##### Broadcast.

Scripts in this category are used to find hosts that may not be specified on the command line using broadcast messages on the network.

##### Brute.

These are scripts that could be used to brute-force authentication on remote servers.

##### Default.

The default scripts associated with nmap find default information for a wide variety of services, from DHCP to DNS to shared directories on Microsoft networks. For example, the following command checks the target system for the Conficker.C worm:

![n map command that checks the target system for the Conficker dot C worm.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM31.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-31)

##### Discovery.

Discovery scripts for nmap can find information associated with a variety of network services, from banners to shared Samba and NFS directories. Discovery scripts include WHOIS information, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) certificates, and more. For example, the following command checks the target system for a list of directories shared over the Samba file service:

![n map command that checks the target system for a list of directories shared over the Samba file service.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM32.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-32)

nmap provides more than just share information. It also includes the version number of the Samba release, the path to the shared directory, anonymous access if allowed, connected users, and more.

##### Denial of service and exploit.

As of this writing, there is one script for both the denial of service (DoS) and exploit categories. The following script reviews a target Samba server for a number of vulnerabilities beyond DoS:

![n map script that reviews a target Samba server for a number of vulnerabilities beyond D o S.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM33.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-33)

##### Exploit.

A limited number of scripts may be used to exploit a vulnerability. An example of this is a check for the Shellshock vulnerability. This script is named http-shellshock.

##### External.

The scripts in the external category are associated with the way servers look to external systems. Many of the scripts in this category can expose risks. For example, the following command determines whether an email server on a remote system is an open relay that can be used by spammers to send messages through your systems:

![n map command that determines whether an email server on a remote system is an open relay that can be used by spammers to send messages through your systems.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM34.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-34)

The following output is associated with a SMTP server on port 25:

![The output of an n map command that is associated with an S M T P server on port 25.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM35.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-5)

##### Fuzzer.

Fuzz attacks on various servers test responses to problems like buffer overflows. So far, nmap includes only one script in this area, on DNS. For example, the following command uses a script to launch a DNS fuzzing attack against an associated server:

![n map command that uses a script to launch a D N S fuzzing attack against an associated server.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM36.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-36)

##### Intrusive.

Many nmap command scripts qualify in both the intrusive and authentication categories. Any attempt to guess usernames and passwords by brute force is an attempt to intrude and test authentication. The following command goes further to see whether the network card associated with the IP address is running in promiscuous mode. If so, an attacker will be able to use a protocol analyzer on the local network:

![n map command that sees whether the network card associated with the I P address is running in promiscuous mode.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM37.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-37)

If the network interface is running in promiscuous mode, which would be the case if you were running a packet-capture program, you may see the following output:

![The output of an n map command if you were running a packet-capture program.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM38.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-38)

##### Malware.

Perhaps this should be a growing category of scripts. For the moment, three have been written for this topic: one each for authentication, web servers, and SMTP servers. The following command checks a web server for known compromises:

![n map command that checks a web server for known compromises.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM39.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-39)

##### Safe.

Scripts in the safe category test the relative safety of named services. As befits this category, it includes several dozen scripts testing the safety of services from the Internet Mail Access Protocol (IMAP) to the LDAP. While a script that tests the capabilities of a Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) server such as Dovecot may not seem to fit the bill, it can reveal features that are unneeded or unused. Such features are frequently ripe for the picking by attackers. The noted script is shown here:

![n map script that checks for the capabilities of a POP 3 server such as Dovecot.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM40.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-40)

The following output excerpt suggests a lot of POP3 features that should be carefully reviewed:

![Excerpt of an n map output that suggests a lot of POP 3 features that should be carefully reviewed.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM41.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-41)

##### Version.

The scripts in this category detect more than just the version number of specific services. Not many scripts exist in this category because the nmap -sV ip_address command does an excellent job detecting the version number and service associated with open ports. However, the following command does provide more information about existing Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol (PPTP) services. In Linux, this is also known as Internet Protocol Security (IPSec).

The scripts in the vulnerability category are all about testing for known vulnerabilities. Expect the number of scripts in this category to grow. The following example tries a known SQL injection on a target HTTP server:

The scripts as listed fall into several categories. Some scripts may fall under multiple categories. Because new scripts and even new switches are under development, assume this is a partial list. For example, a command like the following applies all scripts associated with a scan of the HTTP service:

If the given script is misspelled or is not otherwise available, nmap should return an error with the following message related to the script:

## Running Integrity Checks of Installed Files and Executables

When you have a production system, it’s important to monitor that system for changes. Of course, you should not be alarmed every time a new log is added to the /var/log/ directory. However, changes to critical files such as those in the /boot/ and /sbin/ directories may indicate a problem.

To detect such changes, you need to know how to check the integrity of target systems. Sure, you could just set up a checksum on potentially vulnerable partitions or volumes, but that would be imprecise. If there is a problem, the checksum will not specify the files that have changed.

The first method to check the integrity of a system relates to the integrity of installed packages. To that end, commands based on package-management systems such as the Red Hat Package Manager (rpm) and the Debian package-management program (dpkg) can help.

The default configuration based on a package installation is not precise, however. It highlights problems with normal changes to standard configuration files. Sure, you could keep a list of those changes, but if an attacker were to get into a system and change those files further, there would be no way to tell just using package-management commands. This is the reason behind integrity checkers such as Tripwire and the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE). In general, you will want to use such integrity checkers to log the configuration associated with a gold baseline before putting such systems online. Then you can run the integrity checker on a regular basis. When properly configured, they can highlight any unintended changes to the baseline configuration.

### Verifying a Package

The first method for verifying the integrity of a system is relative to its installed state. With the correct command, you can compare the current list of installed packages with an associated list of installed files. The basic commands vary depending on whether the distribution is built on packages associated with Red Hat or Debian systems.

Note that the use of package-management commands may not provide a complete measure of what is installed. Many enterprising users and administrators install packages more directly from source code, typically collected in a compressed tarball archive. (A tarball is what you call a file that has files or directories collected into a single file by the tar program.)

#### Verifying Ubuntu/Debian Packages

Because Ubuntu is built on Debian Linux, Ubuntu packages are built on the Debian package system. As such, it relies on commands like dpkg and debsums. To obtain a list of currently installed packages on these systems, run the dpkg -1 command. Prepare to be overwhelmed as the list of hundreds or even thousands of packages whizzes by. Of course, the value of such a list is as a database, which you can pipe to a text file or search with the grep command.

One variation on dpkg -1 that provides a more straightforward list of installed packages is as follows:

![A variation of the d p k g hyphen l command that provides a more straightforward list of installed packages.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM46.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-46)

That is just a list of installed packages. When such packages are installed, they include a list of checksums, classified by package, separated by each installed file in the /var/lib/dpkg/info/ directory. To take advantage of that list, run the [debsums](#9781284255935_Glossary.xhtml_gloss-65) command. The debsums command uses Message Digest 5 (MD5) checksums to see if changes have been made to files. The output from the command is impressive. Some desktop systems include a couple of hundred thousand packages or more.

Not all packages include checksum information, however. In addition, some files are configured from a combination of packages, such as the initial RAM disk file in the /boot/ directory. For those files associated with checksums, the only indication of a problem is a FAILED message after the filename.

#### Verifying Red Hat Packages

The Red Hat Package Management system is more precise when it checks the integrity of installed packages. It’s a straightforward command, given the name of a target package. For example, the following command and output is typical for the Postfix email server:

![Command and output that is typical for the Postfix email server.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM47.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-47)

If there were no changes to the files relative to the original package, there would be no output. Eight tests are performed on each file, as described in [Table 13-2](#9781284255935_CH13_03.xhtml_c13-tbl002). The codes would appear from left to right. A dot in place of the code means that the associated test has passed.

TABLE 13-2 Failure codes for rpm -V.

| CODE | DESCRIPTION |
| --- | --- |
| 5 | Checksum associated with the MD5 algorithm |
| S | File size |
| L | Symbolic link |
| T | File modification time |
| D | Device file |
| U | User owner |
| G | Group owner |
| M | File mode |

If a C appears at the end of the failure-code list, the noted file is a configuration file. The output from the rpm -V packagename command can tell you more about the change to the file.

Of course, with hundreds and sometimes thousands of packages on a system, it’s not enough to verify the files associated with one package. Fortunately, the -a switch helps the rpm -ga command check all installed packages. Although changed files are not directly associated with the package, it’s easy to identify the package that owns a file. For example, the following command identifies the package that owns the noted Samba configuration file:

![Command that identifies the package that owns the noted Samba configuration file.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM48.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-48)

As with the debsums command, such checks apply only to packages installed in the rpm package-manager format.

### Performing a Tripwire Check

Tripwire is an intrusion detection system (IDS), with configuration files in the /etc/tripwire/ directory. Briefly, Tripwire can collect information on key files on a computer based on how Tripwire is configured in the twcfg.txt file and the reporting policies documented in the twpol.txt file. When the configuration and policy are set, the following command creates a database of digital checksums for such files in the /var/lib/tripwire/ directory:

![Command that creates a database of digital checksums for files in the var, lib, tripwire directory.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM49.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-49)

Next, you should run the following command to review associated policies. Standard policies for the Tripwire package that you have installed may check on files that do not exist on local systems. Therefore, you should run the following command right away, to modify configuration options and policies to minimize the number of false positives:

![Command that needs to be executed right away to modify configuration options and policies to minimize the number of false positives.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM50.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-50)

For example, the standard Tripwire configuration reports changes in files in the /proc/ and /dev/ directories. Current Linux systems change the contents or access time of numerous files in these directories every time a system is rebooted. Current Linux systems may also change files in the /etc/ directory if the system acquires network address information using DHCP. You can update Tripwire policies with the following command:

![Command to update Tripwire policies.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM51.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-51)

Then the standard Tripwire package is configured to check the local system on a daily basis, courtesy of the tripwire script in the /etc/cron.daily/ directory.

### Testing with the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment

Like Tripwire, AIDE supports periodic checks of installed and configured files. This section goes into a bit more depth on how AIDE works based on information in the aide.conf configuration file. The configuration for Ubuntu and Red Hat systems can vary somewhat. Of course, the details are subject to change, especially if the developers behind one distribution decide that the approach of the other distribution is better. In either case, AIDE rules are defined with attributes as described in [Table 13-3](#9781284255935_CH13_03.xhtml_c13-tbl003).

Some developers consider AIDE to be superior to Tripwire. In fact, AIDE packages are available from the main Ubuntu repository and supported Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) repositories. Therefore, the installation of AIDE is supported at least in some ways by developers for both distributions.

#### Ubuntu AIDE

When installed on Ubuntu systems, AIDE is configured in files in the /etc/aide/ directory. In addition, per the /etc/default/aide file, configuration options for individual services are defined in files in the /etc/aide/aide.conf.d/ directory. Although the basic database files are similar, Ubuntu’s version includes directives with combinations of default codes in the main /etc/aide/aide.conf file. For example, the following directive suggests that AIDE can use a variety of checksums for every file. Each of the options listed is described in [Table 13-3](#9781284255935_CH13_03.xhtml_c13-tbl003).

## Ensuring That Security Does Not Prevent Legitimate Access

It’s possible to configure too much security on a system. In the area of passwords, if the requirements are too strict, users are more likely to forget their passwords. Users will then either overload administrators with password-reset requests or write their passwords next to their workstations. Neither situation promotes true computer security. In the following sections, you will look at reasonable password policies, how you can implement them in the shadow password suite with the chage command, and how you can regulate access with pluggable authentication modules (PAMs).

### Reasonable Password Policies

In an ideal world, users would frequently change their passwords. After all, if the lifetime of a password were less than the time it takes for an attacker to decipher the password, then you could keep password-authentication databases out in the open! It’s not, however, an ideal world.

In addition to needing to change passwords to prevent them from being cracked, you should change them so that if a password is cracked, the attacker has access to the account for only a limited time. This is less relevant if the account has permissions to create users or access can be escalated to create users. This is because an attacker may simply create his or her own account rather than continuing to use a compromised account. Of course, a new account can be noticed, so it’s not a guarantee that a new account will be created.

The best passwords are passphrases, which can be complete sentences. Many authentication systems do not support options such as spaces in a password, however. Other than a passphrase, the best password is a combination of uppercase and lowercase characters, along with numbers and punctuation. You want users to be able to remember their passwords without having to write them down, however. In recent years, NIST had changed its guidance regarding passwords. The document that is currently used to provide guidance to authentication practices is Special Publication 800-63B. This document requires passwords be a minimum of eight characters but any system that uses passwords should be able to support passwords to 64 characters in length. NIST has moved away from frequent password rotation, instead recommending stronger passphrases be used.

In organizations where security is important, such as intelligence agencies, users generally have a greater understanding of the need for password security. You should be able to set more rigorous requirements in such cases. The challenge is to have a balanced password policy. If you make the policy too restrictive with regular changes and complexity requirements, people may end up writing their passwords down. If users are writing their passwords down just to keep up with draconian policies, the password policy will not be protecting systems or the information stored on them. It’s important to keep the goal of a policy in mind. The goal should be to protect unauthorized access to your systems.

You can configure account policies for a specific account with the chage command. The current settings are defined in the output to the chage -1 username command. [Table 13-4](#9781284255935_CH13_04.xhtml_c13-tbl004) shows the output and associated chage command options. You would not use chage to set the actual password policies, which would include complexity requirements and length. That would be configured with the PAM settings.

When applicable, the date can be set in YYYY-MM-DD format. The password expiration date is based on the value of the “maximum number of days between password change” setting associated with the -M days switch shown in [Table 13-4](#9781284255935_CH13_04.xhtml_c13-tbl004).

TABLE 13-4 Command options for chage.

| OUTPUT | COMMAND OPTION |
| --- | --- |
| Last password change | -d YYYY-MM-DD |
| Password expires | N/A |
| Password inactive | -I YYYY-MM-DD |
| Account expires | -E YYYY-MM-DD |
| Minimum number of days between password change | -m days |
| Maximum number of days between password change | -M days |
| Number of days of warning before password expires | -W days |

In addition, it’s possible to set requirements for password complexity with the help of PAMs. The key file is /etc/pam.d/passwd. Password complexity requires the use of the pam_cracklib and pam_unix modules. On Red Hat systems, you can find the key directive either in the system-auth or passwd-auth file in the /etc/pam.d/ directory. As suggested by the last directive on the line, three login attempts are allowed. While the cracklib library may be installed, this line may not be in place in the file so if you want to ensure passwords are verified against password complexity rules and well-known passwords, you can add this line.

![Line that needs to be added, if you want to ensure passwords are verified against password complexity rules and well-known passwords.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM59.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-59)

On Ubuntu systems, cracklib may also not be installed by default. If it is not installed and you want to enforce password policies, you would need to install the pamlib-cracklib package. This should include a line like the one below in the file common-password.

![The line that needs to be included in the common-password file on Ubuntu systems.](images/9781284255935_CH13_CUM60.jpg)
[Description](9781284255935_Alt.xhtml_summary-cd13-60)

As suggested by the directives in the line, the minimum password length is six alpha-numeric characters. The difok=3 option means that new passwords must have at least three characters different from the current password. [Table 13-5](#9781284255935_CH13_04.xhtml_c13-tbl005) lists options that support password complexity.

TABLE 13-5 Password complexity options for pam_cracklib.so and pam_unix.so.

| OPTION | DESCRIPTION |
| --- | --- |
| minlen | Minimum password length, in alphanumeric characters. |
| dcredit | Minimum number of digits in a password, in negative numbers. |
| lcredit | Minimum number of lowercase letters in a password, in negative numbers. |
| ocredit | Minimum number of other characters in a new password, in negative numbers. |
| retry | Number of tries allowed to confirm when changing a password. |
| nullok | Blank password allowed. |
| remember=n | n previous passwords are remembered; a repeat of from that list of passwords is not allowed. |
| obscure | A given password is compared to a previous password to make sure it’s not a palindrome, different only with respect to case, or otherwise too similar. |

You can regulate access by adding an appropriate module to the /etc/pam.d login configuration file. Specifically, the following account module supports access limits through the /etc/security/access.conf file:
